Lecture 48

Moving endpoints, transversality and Fermat’s principle

We derive the boundary term before imposing endpoint restrictions. We distinguish a change at fixed coordinate from a moving point’s total change, classify the stationary free-end Dido arcs, and derive reflection and refraction laws.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Derive natural conditions for free endpoint values of a C2C^2C2 candidate.
  • Classify free-end Dido extremals among regular C2C^2C2 parametrised curves.
  • Derive the general first variation and apply transversality to an endpoint constrained to a curve.
  • Derive an optical junction law and distinguish a stationary optical path from a shortest path.

Lecture 47 fixed both coordinates of each endpoint. Allowing an endpoint to move adds conditions to the differential equation. The stages here are free endpoint values and Dido (Sections 48.1–48.2), moving integration endpoints and transversality (Sections 48.3–48.4), then Fermat’s principle and optical interfaces (Section 48.5).

48.2 Free-end Dido with parametrised curves

48.3 Variable integration endpoints

Free values on a fixed interval do not change its integration limits. We now allow both limits to move. Return to nnn dependent functions and the integrand F∈C2(U;R)F\in C^2(U;\R)F∈C2(U;R) of Section 48.1.

Definition 48.4 (Endpoint family). An endpoint family consists of an open interval III, a number ϵ0>0\epsilon_0>0ϵ0​>0, a map (x,ϵ)⟼yϵ(x):I×(−ϵ0,ϵ0)⟶Rn,(x,\epsilon)\longmapsto\vv y_\epsilon(x): I\times(-\epsilon_0,\epsilon_0)\longrightarrow\R^n,(x,ϵ)⟼yϵ​(x):I×(−ϵ0​,ϵ0​)⟶Rn, and C1C^1C1 functions aϵ<bϵa_\epsilon<b_\epsilonaϵ​<bϵ​ with values in III. The map, its first partial derivatives, and both mixed derivatives exist and are continuous. The mixed derivatives agree. For every parameter, (x,yϵ,∂xyϵ)∈U(x,\vv y_\epsilon,\partial_x\vv y_\epsilon)\in U(x,yϵ​,∂x​yϵ​)∈U on [aϵ,bϵ][a_\epsilon,b_\epsilon][aϵ​,bϵ​].

A C2C^2C2 map meets the mixed-derivative requirement by Schwarz’s theorem (GM 37). So does yˉ+ϵη\bar{\vv y}+\epsilon\vv\etayˉ​+ϵη with yˉ∈C2(I;Rn)\bar{\vv y}\in C^2(I;\R^n)yˉ​∈C2(I;Rn) and η∈C1(I;Rn)\vv\eta\in C^1(I;\R^n)η∈C1(I;Rn). 48.5 Fermat’s principle and optical interfaces

From here nnn denotes the refractive index, not a number of dependent functions. We use one dependent function. The index is n=c/(local light speed)>0n=c/(\text{local light speed})>0n=c/(local light speed)>0, where ccc is the vacuum light speed. For a graph, optical length and travel time are J[y]=∫abn(x,y)1+y′2 ⁣dx,travel time=J[y]c.J[y]=\int_a^b n(x,y)\sqrt{1+y'^2}\dd x,\qquad \text{travel time}=\frac{J[y]}c.J[y]=∫ab​n(x,y)1+y′2​dx,travel time=cJ[y]​.(48.23) The length element is  ⁣ds=1+y′2 ⁣dx\dd s=\sqrt{1+y'^2}\dd xds=1+y′2​dx.

J[y]=∫abn(x,y)1+y′2 ⁣dx,travel time=J[y]c.J[y]=\int_a^b n(x,y)\sqrt{1+y'^2}\dd x,\qquad \text{travel time}=\frac{J[y]}c.J[y]=∫ab​n(x,y)1+y′2​dx,travel time=cJ[y]​.(48.23)

Fermat’s principle (modelling postulate). In geometrical optics, a ray makes optical length stationary among admissible paths with the same endpoints. At an interface or a mirror, the competing paths are also required to meet the interface or mirror, as the ray does. This physical postulate is unrelated to GM 9’s Fermat theorem about the derivative at an interior extremum. In a homogeneous medium, nnn is constant and Lecture 46’s length equation makes each smooth ray segment straight. At a discontinuity of nnn, the smooth equation alone cannot join the two segments.

Figure 48.2 fixes the angle convention and the data used below.

The reflected broken line just found has length 5+5=105+5=105+5=10. The direct segment from (−3,4)(-3,4)(−3,4) to (3,4)(3,4)(3,4) has length 666. It does not touch the reflecting line and belongs to a different admissible class. Fermat’s postulate asserts stationarity, and Lecture 46 showed that a stationary path need not be a minimum.

Summary

The boundary term determines which endpoint condition accompanies Euler–Lagrange. A free value on a fixed interval gives a natural condition. A moving end requires its total change as well as its shape variation. The same calculation determines contact with a curve and an optical junction.

  • Natural conditions: at a C2C^2C2 stationary path, the derivative of the integrand with respect to yj′y_j'yj′​ vanishes at each free endpoint value yjy_jyj​. For a normal constrained stationary path, use the augmented integrand.

  • Dido: regular C2C^2C2 free-end extremals run monotonically through mmm half-turns of a circle centred on the axis, with signed area ±ℓ2/(2πm)\pm\ell^2/(2\pi m)±ℓ2/(2πm). The semicircle has the largest signed area among these extremals.

  • Moving ends: Δy=δy+y′Δx\Delta y=\delta y+y'\Delta xΔy=δy+y′Δx converts the shape form into the total form of the general first variation.

  • Optics: the junction law gives Snell’s law and equal reflection angles. A stationary reflected path need not be the shortest path between its endpoints.

Lecture 49 takes time as the independent variable and develops particle action.

References

Preparation: Lecture 22 (rule I2), Lecture 29 (closed-box lemma), Lectures 46–47 (first variation, fundamental lemma, coupled Euler–Lagrange equations, Euler’s constrained-variation theorem and Dido); GM 9 (monotonicity, constancy and bounds; Fermat’s theorem), GM 11 (matching derivatives at a point), GM 26 (an integral with a moving endpoint; definite substitution and integration by parts), GM 28 (arc length), GM 36 (continuous partial derivatives imply differentiability; the matrix chain rule), GM 37 (Schwarz’s theorem; implicit function theorem).

Reading: I. M. Gelfand and S. V. Hobson and S. J. Bence, Mathematical Methods for Physics and Engineering, 3rd ed., §22.3.4, pp. 782–785 (variable endpoints), and §22.5.1, pp. 787–788 (Fermat’s principle and refraction).
